meta.title: ISTQB CTFL v4.0 — Foundation Level Syllabus
meta.author: Companion: Lucjan Stapp, Adam Roman & Michael Pilaeten (Springer Self-Study Guide)
meta.description: One topic per official ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level (CTFL) syllabus v4.0 section, with self-check prompts and AI-generated exam-prep notes. Section descriptions and self-check items are written from the public ISTQB syllabus outline, not copied from any book — use it alongside the Springer self-study guide (or any CTFL v4.0 book) as your primary reading.

topics.title: 1.1 What is Testing?
topics.module: ISTQB CTFL v4.0 — Chapter 1: Fundamentals of Testing
topics.description: Defines what software testing actually is, distinguishes it from debugging, and introduces the common objectives of a test activity (finding defects, gaining confidence, preventing defects, providing information for decisions).
topics.notes: 📘 Study companion: ISTQB® CTFL – A Self-Study Guide (Syllabus v4.0) by Stapp, Roman & Pilaeten (Springer). Read the '1.1 What is Testing?' section there, then use 'Generate AI Content' below for exam-style notes and practice questions. Self-check items are study prompts aligned to the public ISTQB syllabus outline — verify exact LO codes/K-levels against the current syllabus PDF at istqb.org.

questions.text: Can you define 'testing' in your own words and explain how it differs from 'debugging'?
Can you list the typical objectives of testing (defect detection, confidence building, defect prevention, decision support)?
Can you explain how testing objectives differ depending on the context (e.g. component testing vs acceptance testing)?

topics.title: 1.2 Why is Testing Necessary?
topics.module: ISTQB CTFL v4.0 — Chapter 1: Fundamentals of Testing
topics.description: Covers testing's contribution to quality and to building confidence, the relationship between errors/defects/failures/root causes, and the concept of 'enough' testing given risk and constraints.
topics.notes: 📘 Study companion: ISTQB® CTFL – A Self-Study Guide (Syllabus v4.0) by Stapp, Roman & Pilaeten (Springer). Read the '1.2 Why is Testing Necessary?' section there, then use 'Generate AI Content' below. Self-check items are study prompts aligned to the public ISTQB syllabus outline — verify exact LO codes/K-levels against the current syllabus PDF at istqb.org.

questions.text: Can you explain the difference between an error (mistake), a defect (fault/bug), and a failure?
Can you describe how testing supports both quality assurance and quality control?
Can you explain what determines 'how much testing is enough' for a given project?

topics.title: 1.3 Testing Principles
topics.module: ISTQB CTFL v4.0 — Chapter 1: Fundamentals of Testing
topics.description: The seven well-known testing principles: testing shows presence of defects, exhaustive testing is impossible, early testing saves time/money, defect clustering, pesticide paradox, testing is context dependent, and the absence-of-errors fallacy.
topics.notes: 📘 Study companion: ISTQB® CTFL – A Self-Study Guide (Syllabus v4.0) by Stapp, Roman & Pilaeten (Springer). Read the '1.3 Testing Principles' section there, then use 'Generate AI Content' below. Self-check items are study prompts aligned to the public ISTQB syllabus outline — verify exact wording/order of the 7 principles against the current syllabus PDF at istqb.org.

questions.text: Can you list and briefly explain all seven testing principles from memory?
Can you give a real (or realistic) example for the 'pesticide paradox' and the 'defect clustering' principle?
Can you explain why 'testing shows presence of defects, not their absence' matters for how you report test results?

topics.title: 1.4 Test Process
topics.module: ISTQB CTFL v4.0 — Chapter 1: Fundamentals of Testing
topics.description: The test process in context: test planning, monitoring & control, analysis, design, implementation, execution, and completion — plus the key test work products each activity produces and how traceability links them to test basis items.
topics.notes: 📘 Study companion: ISTQB® CTFL – A Self-Study Guide (Syllabus v4.0) by Stapp, Roman & Pilaeten (Springer). Self-check items are study prompts aligned to the public ISTQB syllabus outline — verify exact LO codes/K-levels against the current syllabus PDF at istqb.org.

questions.text: Can you list the test process activities in order and describe what each one produces?
Can you explain why these activities are often iterative/overlapping rather than strictly sequential?
Can you explain what traceability is and why it matters between test basis, test conditions, and test cases?

topics.title: 1.5 The Psychology of Testing
topics.module: ISTQB CTFL v4.0 — Chapter 1: Fundamentals of Testing
topics.description: Human factors in testing: the mindset difference between testers and developers, confirmation bias, and communicating defects/test results constructively.
topics.notes: 📘 Study companion: ISTQB® CTFL – A Self-Study Guide (Syllabus v4.0) by Stapp, Roman & Pilaeten (Springer). Can you describe how to phrase a defect report so it stays factual and doesn't feel like a personal attack?

topics.title: 2.1 Testing in the Context of a Software Development Lifecycle
topics.module: ISTQB CTFL v4.0 — Chapter 2: Testing Throughout the SDLC
topics.description: How testing fits into different development models (sequential/V-model style vs iterative/incremental vs Agile), the importance of good test-ware, and how organizational context (e.g. DevOps) shapes testing.
topics.notes: 📘 Study companion: ISTQB® CTFL – A Self-Study Guide (Syllabus v4.0) by Stapp, Roman & Pilaeten (Springer). Read the '2.1' section there, then use 'Generate AI Content' below. Can you describe how testing activities change in an iterative/incremental or Agile context?
Can you explain what 'good test-ware' looks like (maintainable, traceable, reusable) and why it matters long-term?

topics.title: 2.2 Test Levels and Test Types
topics.module: ISTQB CTFL v4.0 — Chapter 2: Testing Throughout the SDLC
topics.description: The four classic test levels (component, integration, system, acceptance) and the four test types (functional, non-functional, white-box, and change-related/confirmation & regression testing), including how they relate to each other.
topics.notes: 📘 Study companion: ISTQB® CTFL – A Self-Study Guide (Syllabus v4.0) by Stapp, Roman & Pilaeten (Springer). Read the '2.2' section there, then use 'Generate AI Content' below. questions.text: Can you name all four test levels and describe the typical objective and typical owner of each?
Can you distinguish functional testing from non-functional testing, with an example of each?
Can you explain the difference between confirmation (re-)testing and regression testing?
Can you describe what acceptance testing typically checks for, and who is usually involved?

topics.title: 2.3 Maintenance Testing
topics.module: ISTQB CTFL v4.0 — Chapter 2: Testing Throughout the SDLC

Can you explain what impact analysis is and how it decides the scope of regression testing after a change?

topics.module: ISTQB CTFL v4.0 — Chapter 3: Static Testing
topics.description: The formal review process (planning, kick-off, individual review, review meeting, rework, follow-up), the roles involved (author, moderator, reviewers, scribe), and review types from informal to formal inspection.

topics.title: 4.1 Test Techniques Overview
topics.module: ISTQB CTFL v4.0 — Chapter 4: Test Analysis and Design
topics.description: The three categories of test technique — black-box, white-box, and experience-based — and how choosing between them relates to what you're trying to cover and what you know about the system internals.
topics.notes: 📘 Study companion: ISTQB® CTFL – A Self-Study Guide (Syllabus v4.0) by Stapp, Roman & Pilaeten (Springer). Read the '4.1' section there, then use 'Generate AI Content' below. Self-check items are study prompts aligned to the public ISTQB syllabus outline — verify exact LO codes/K-levels against the current syllabus PDF at istqb.org.

questions.text: Can you explain the difference between black-box, white-box, and experience-based techniques?
Can you describe what 'coverage' means in testing, and why 100% coverage of any single measure isn't the same as complete testing?

topics.title: 4.2 Black-Box Test Techniques
topics.module: ISTQB CTFL v4.0 — Chapter 4: Test Analysis and Design
topics.description: Equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision table testing, state transition testing, and black-box variants like use case testing and (for CTFL, briefly) domain testing — how to derive test cases without looking at the code.
topics.notes: 📘 Study companion: ISTQB® CTFL – A Self-Study Guide (Syllabus v4.0) by Stapp, Roman & Pilaeten (Springer). Read the '4.2' section there — this is one of the most exam-heavy sections, expect several worked examples in the book. Then use 'Generate AI Content' below for extra practice questions. Self-check items are study prompts aligned to the public ISTQB syllabus outline — verify exact LO codes/K-levels against the current syllabus PDF at istqb.org.

questions.text: Given a simple input range, can you derive equivalence partitions and pick representative test values?
Can you apply boundary value analysis to a range and identify the correct boundary values (including off-by-one edge cases)?
Given a small set of conditions and actions, can you build a decision table and derive test cases from it?
Given a simple state diagram, can you derive test cases covering states, transitions, and invalid transitions?

topics.title: 4.3 White-Box Test Techniques
topics.module: ISTQB CTFL v4.0 — Chapter 4: Test Analysis and Design
topics.description: Statement testing/coverage and branch/decision testing/coverage — deriving test cases from the code's control flow and calculating coverage percentages.
topics.notes: 📘 Study companion: ISTQB® CTFL – A Self-Study Guide (Syllabus v4.0) by Stapp, Roman & Pilaeten (Springer). Read the '4.3' section there and practice the coverage-calculation examples by hand. Then use 'Generate AI Content' below. Self-check items are study prompts aligned to the public ISTQB syllabus outline — verify exact LO codes/K-levels against the current syllabus PDF at istqb.org.

questions.text: Given simple pseudocode, can you calculate statement coverage for a given set of test cases?
Given simple pseudocode with an if/else, can you calculate branch/decision coverage and identify which test cases are missing?
Can you explain why 100% branch coverage implies 100% statement coverage but not vice versa?

topics.title: 4.4 Experience-Based Test Techniques
topics.module: ISTQB CTFL v4.0 — Chapter 4: Test Analysis and Design
topics.description: Error guessing, exploratory testing (session-based approaches, charters), and checklist-based testing — techniques that rely on tester skill, intuition, and experience rather than a formal model.
topics.notes: 📘 Study companion: ISTQB® CTFL – A Self-Study Guide (Syllabus v4.0) by Stapp, Roman & Pilaeten (Springer). Read the '4.4' section there, then use 'Generate AI Content' below. Can you describe exploratory testing and what a 'test charter' defines in a session-based approach?
Can you explain when checklist-based testing is a good fit versus a risk (e.g. becoming stale)?

topics.title: 4.5 Collaboration-Based Test Approaches
topics.module: ISTQB CTFL v4.0 — Chapter 4: Test Analysis and Design
